options.text: 91 cm is the minimum/standard requirement
91 cm is the maximum permitted value
91 cm applies only to specific conditions
91 cm is an approximate value subject to interpretation

questions.text: Under RA 9514 RIRR (2019), Rule 8, what is the minimum retail aisle width when seating exceeds 50 persons on both sides of a single central aisle?

options.text: 76 cm (760 mm) — the base aisle width applicable to all retail configurations
91 cm (910 mm) — the threshold for aisles with seating on one side only
122 cm (1,220 mm) — required when seating exceeds 50 persons on both sides
112 cm (1,120 mm) — the business occupancy egress corridor minimum per PD 1096

rationale.summary: RA 9514 RIRR Rule 8 sets 122 cm as the minimum for aisles with seating on both sides exceeding 50.
rationale.explanation: The aisle width progression under RA 9514 RIRR Rule 8 is: 76 cm (≤50 seats, one side) → 91 cm (>50 seats, one side) → 122 cm (>50 seats, both sides). Option A is the base for low-density one-side seating. Option B applies to one-side seating only. Option D is the office/business corridor minimum from PD 1096, not a retail aisle dimension.
common_misconceptions: Applying the one-side aisle threshold (91 cm) to both-sides seating scenarios
Confusing PD 1096 egress corridor minimums with RA 9514 retail aisle requirements

questions.explanation: This question tests recall of the RA 9514 retail aisle width progression.

questions.text: A restaurant in Manila has 60 dining tables. Under BP 344 IRR, how many tables must be accessible, and what is the required table height?

options.text: 6 tables (10% of 60) at a table height of 750 mm above finished floor
6 tables (10% of 60) at a table height of 720 mm above finished floor
3 tables (5% of 60) at a table height of 750 mm above finished floor
3 tables (5% of 60) at a table height of 710–865 mm above finished floor

rationale.summary: BP 344 requires 10% of tables to be accessible at 750 mm height. 10% of 60 = 6 tables.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 IRR Sec. 7 mandates at least 10% of all dining tables must be accessible — 10% of 60 = 6 tables. The prescribed table height is 750 mm. Option A applies the ADA's 5% seating-space rate, not BP 344's table-based rate. Option B uses the correct percentage but an incorrect table height (720 mm is not a BP 344 value). Option D applies both ADA's 5% and ADA's height range (710–865 mm), which are US standards.
common_misconceptions: Using the ADA 5% seating-space rate when the applicable code is BP 344 (which uses 10% of tables)
Citing 720 mm as the BP 344 table height — the correct value is 750 mm

questions.explanation: This question tests application of BP 344 accessible dining requirements including table count and height.

questions.text: Under ADA 2010 Section 226.1, what percentage of seating spaces in a US restaurant must comply with accessible dining surface requirements, and how does this compare to BP 344?

options.text: ADA requires 10% of seating spaces; BP 344 also requires 10% of tables — both are identical
ADA requires 5% of seating spaces; BP 344 requires 10% of tables — the percentages and counting units differ
ADA requires 5% of tables; BP 344 requires 10% of seating spaces — the standards are reversed
ADA requires 10% of tables; BP 344 requires 5% of seating spaces — the Philippines is less stringent

rationale.summary: ADA §226.1 requires 5% of seating/standing spaces; BP 344 requires 10% of tables — different percentages and different units of measurement.
rationale.explanation: ADA 2010 Section 226.1 specifies 'at least 5% of seating spaces and standing spaces' must comply. BP 344 IRR Sec. 7 specifies 'at least 10% of tables.' These use different base units: ADA counts individual seats/spaces; BP 344 counts tables. The mnemonic is 'ADA is half of BP' — 5% vs 10%. Options A, C, and D all swap, equalize, or reverse the values incorrectly.
common_misconceptions: Assuming both codes measure the same unit (tables vs. seating spaces is the critical distinction)
Thinking the ADA and BP 344 percentages are equal when they differ by a factor of two

questions.text: PD 1096 specifies a minimum egress corridor width for Business Occupancy office spaces. What is this dimension, and what is its US equivleant under IBC?

options.text: PH: 0.90 m (900 mm); US: 36 in (914 mm) — both are accessible route minimums
PH: 1.22 m (1,220 mm); US: 48 in (121.9 cm) — the both-sides retail aisle standard applied to offices
PH: 1.12 m (1,120 mm); US: 44 in (111.8 cm) — nearly identical egress corridor minimums
PH: 1.50 m (1,500 mm); US: 60 in (152.4 cm) — the passing-space standard for dual wheelchair clearance

rationale.summary: PD 1096 mandates 1.12 m for business occupancy egress corridors; the US IBC §1005/OSHA equivalent is 44 in (111.8 cm) — virtually identical.
rationale.explanation: PD 1096 Table 602-A establishes 1.12 m (1,120 mm) as the minimum egress corridor for Business Occupancy. The IBC/OSHA standard for commercial occupancies is 44 inches (111.8 cm / 1,118 mm) — nearly the same. Option A gives the accessible route minimum (ADA 36 in / BP 344 900 mm), not the egress corridor. Option C is the retail both-sides aisle dimension. Option D is the ADA passing space for two wheelchair users.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the accessible route minimum (900 mm) with the egress corridor minimum (1,120 mm)
Thinking PH and US office corridor standards are significantly different when they are nearly equivalent

questions.explanation: This question tests knowledge of office corridor minimums under Philippine and US codes.

questions.text: BP 344 IRR (Amended), Section 7 requires accessible dining tables in Philippine restaurants. Which set of knee clearance dimensions is correct under BP 344?

options.text: Height: 685 mm, Width: 760 mm, Depth: 483 mm — the ADA 2010 knee clearance standard
Height: 700 mm, Width: 760 mm, Depth: 480 mm — combining BP 344 height with ADA width
Height: 720 mm, Width: 800 mm, Depth: 480 mm — derived from Filipino seated knee height data
Height: 700 mm, Width: 800 mm, Depth: 480 mm — the BP 344 IRR knee clearance standard

rationale.summary: BP 344 IRR Sec. 7 specifies knee clearance of 700 mm H × 800 mm W × 480 mm D.
rationale.explanation: The BP 344 mnemonic is '7-8-4-8': 700 mm Height / 800 mm Width / 480 mm Depth / table at 750 mm. Option A is the US ADA 2010 standard (27 in × 30 in × 19 in = 685 × 760 × 483 mm). Option C uses an incorrect 720 mm height. Option D mixes the BP 344 height with the narrower ADA width.
common_misconceptions: Substituting ADA's 685 mm knee clearance height for BP 344's 700 mm in Philippine exam answers
Confusing the 760 mm ADA width with BP 344's wider 800 mm requirement

questions.explanation: This question tests recall of BP 344 knee clearance dimensions versus the ADA standard.

questions.text: An architect states that '91 cm equals 915 mm' when converting a retail aisle dimension for construction documents. Why is this a critical error on the LEA?

options.text: 915 mm is the IBC minimum aisle, not the RA 9514 value, so the citation is jurisdictionally wrong and could lead to non-compliance
The error is minor — 915 mm and 910 mm are both within the permitted tolerance range for aisle widths, thus not affecting the overall design
The correct conversion is 91 cm = 9,100 mm; the error is a decimal place mistake rather than a unit error, which could cause significant miscalculations
91 cm equals 910 mm, not 915 mm; 915 mm is a different, non-standard dimension that misrepresents the code requirement

rationale.summary: 91 cm × 10 mm/cm = 910 mm. Stating 915 mm is a unit conversion error that misquotes the code dimension.
rationale.explanation: The conversion is: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 91 cm = 91 × 10 = 910 mm exactly. 915 mm = 91.5 cm — a completely different measurement. On the ALE, presenting an incorrect unit conversion when citing a code dimension is treated as a factual error. Option A is wrong — the 914 mm figure is the ADA accessible route width, not the IBC aisle minimum. Option C has an entirely wrong decimal. Option D incorrectly implies a tolerance applies to this specific code citation.
common_misconceptions: Rounding 910 mm upward to 915 mm, creating a non-existent code dimension
Assuming small millimeter differences are insignificant on code compliance questions

questions.explanation: This question tests the common unit conversion error (91 cm ≠ 915 mm) flagged as a critical error in the source article.

questions.text: A restaurant in Pasig City has a single central aisle with 80 fixed seats on one side and an aisle length of 10 meters to the nearest exit. What is the minimum aisle width under RA 9514 RIRR (2019), Rule 8?

options.text: 91 cm — seats exceed 50 on one side; no length increment applies under Rule 8
116 cm — base 91 cm for one-side seating plus 25 cm length increment for 10 meters
122 cm — the both-sides threshold automatically applies whenever seats exceed 50
76 cm — the base retail aisle width regardless of seat count applies here

rationale.summary: Base 91 cm (>50 seats, one side) plus 10 m × 2.5 cm/m = 25 cm length increment = 116 cm total.
rationale.explanation: Step 1: >50 seats on ONE side → base = 91 cm. Step 2: Length increment = 10 m × 2.5 cm/m = 25 cm. Step 3: Total = 91 + 25 = 116 cm. Option A ignores the mandatory length increment. Option C wrongly applies the both-sides threshold to a one-side scenario. Option D applies the base aisle regardless of seat count, which is incorrect once seats exceed 50.
common_misconceptions: Forgetting to apply the +2.5 cm per meter length increment toward exits
Applying the 122 cm both-sides threshold when seating is only on one side

questions.explanation: This question tests application of the RA 9514 aisle width calculation including the length increment.

questions.text: A restaurant in BGC has 65 fixed seats arranged on both sides of a single aisle that runs 8 meters to the nearest exit. What is the minimum aisle width under RA 9514 RIRR (2019), Rule 8?

options.text: 142 cm — both-sides base (122 cm) plus length increment (8 m × 2.5 cm/m = 20 cm)
91 cm — seats exceed 50 but only the one-side threshold is triggered by the layout described
122 cm — the both-sides base width applies; length increments are not added under Rule 8
136 cm — one-side base (91 cm) plus length increment (8 m × 2.5 cm/m = 20 cm) plus 25 cm buffer

rationale.summary: Base 122 cm (>50 seats, both sides) plus 8 m × 2.5 cm/m = 20 cm increment = 142 cm total.
rationale.explanation: Step 1: 65 seats > 50, arranged on BOTH sides → base = 122 cm. Step 2: Length increment = 8 m × 2.5 cm/m = 20 cm. Step 3: Total = 122 + 20 = 142 cm. Option A omits the mandatory length increment. Option B wrongly uses the one-side threshold. Option D applies an incorrect formula mixing multiple figures.
common_misconceptions: Stopping at the base width without applying the aisle-length increment
Using the one-side threshold (91 cm) instead of the both-sides threshold (122 cm) when seats are on both sides

questions.explanation: This question tests the full RA 9514 aisle calculation combining the both-sides base width and length increment.

questions.text: A Philippine architect designing an accessible dining area is told to 'use whichever accessibility standard is more stringent.' Comparing ADA 2010 and BP 344 for knee clearance height under dining tables, which standard requires greater clearance?

options.text: ADA 2010 requires greater clearance at 27 inches (685 mm), which exceeds BP 344's 700 mm height
Both standards require identical knee clearance height — the 685 mm and 700 mm values are considered equivalent
BP 344 requires greater clearance at 700 mm height, compared to ADA's 27 inches (685 mm) height
ADA requires 685 mm and BP 344 requires 680 mm; ADA is marginally more stringent

rationale.summary: BP 344 requires 700 mm knee clearance height vs. ADA's 27 inches (685 mm) — BP 344 is more generous and more demanding.
rationale.explanation: ADA 2010 §306.3 requires a minimum knee clearance height of 27 inches = 685 mm. BP 344 IRR Sec. 7 requires 700 mm — 15 mm higher. Despite Filipino users having smaller sitting knee heights (PH male 95th% = 55.9 cm vs. US 61.6 cm), BP 344 sets a higher clearance because it is designed for wheelchair users, and takes a conservative approach. When 'more stringent' means larger clearance, BP 344's 700 mm governs. Option A incorrectly states that 685 mm exceeds 700 mm.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that because Filipino bodies are smaller, BP 344 would require less clearance than ADA
Treating 685 mm and 700 mm as interchangeable when they are distinct code values

questions.explanation: This question tests comparative analysis of ADA and BP 344 knee clearance requirements.

questions.text: A designer argues that since Filipino mlea 95th percentile sitting knee height is only 55.9 cm, the BP 344 knee clearance of 700 mm is excessively generous for ambulatory Filipino users. What is the most accurate evaluation of this argument?

options.text: The argument is correct — BP 344 should be reduced to 560 mm to match the 95th percentile Filipino knee height, which is a common suggestion
The argument misidentifies the design user — BP 344's 700 mm is designed for wheelchair users whose thigh and footrest clearance requirements differ from ambulatory users
The argument is correct — the 700 mm figure is a transcription error from the ADA; it should be 685 mm, which is a frequent claim
The argument is partially correct — BP 344 should use the 5th percentile Filipino female knee height of 42.2 cm as the governing dimension, which is often debated

rationale.summary: BP 344's 700 mm knee clearance is designed for wheelchair users, not ambulatory Filipino users — the ambulatory knee height data is irrelevant to this requirement.
rationale.explanation: The critical insight from the article: 'BP 344 is designed to accommodate wheelchair users whose knee height (with footrests) may differ from ambulatory users.' The Filipino male 95th percentile ambulatory knee height of 55.9 cm (559 mm) is well below BP 344's 700 mm — meaning ambulatory users have ample clearance. The constraint is wheelchair geometry, not ambulatory knee height. Reducing the standard based on ambulatory data would exclude wheelchair users. Options A and D misapply ambulatory data to a wheelchair-use standard. Option C is factually wrong — 700 mm is the correct BP 344 value.
common_misconceptions: Applying ambulatory body dimension data to a standard designed specifically for wheelchair user clearance
Confusing the Filipino ambulatory knee height with the wheelchair-user clearance requirement

questions.explanation: This question tests critical evaluation of anthropometric reasoning applied to accessibility code requirements.
